claim.text: Most Massachusetts legislative races have no real choice on the ballot, and Question 3 would change that.

scripts.title: Uncontested
scripts.framing: Leads with the number. Good if you want a hard fact up front.
scripts.source: Parallax Partner Portal Lite script library (full text from the library's editor screen)
scripts.text:
Flip a coin. That’s your odds of your state legislative race actually being contested in Massachusetts.
Since 2014, 51% of races in this state — more than half — have had just ONE name on the ballot. No opponent. No debate. No choice.
Massachusetts ranks dead last in the country for electoral competitiveness.
That’s not democracy, that’s your leaders being chosen for you.
And it’s not because good candidates don’t exist — it’s because the system makes it nearly impossible for a challenger to even get on the ballot in the first place.
So every two years, the same seats go back to the same people, and nobody has to explain a single vote. Voters show up… to rubber-stamp a decision that was already made for them.

why.note: “Flip a coin” turns the statistic into odds a viewer can feel before a single number is said — the concrete, curiosity-first opening that won the randomized headline tests.

The number lands in the second line and is repeated three ways — no opponent, no debate, no choice. A fact most viewers haven't heard is one of the few script choices that paid off on favorability. Parallax's 51% is kept verbatim; the returns PAX2 holds put it at 62.8% — 628 of the last 1,000 races.
Anger on purpose: “chosen for you,” “rubber-stamp.” Angry ads ran ahead on favorability; on vote choice the tests can't tell.

The only script in the library that never asks for the vote — it ends on the bleak note instead. In the vote-choice tests, saying the ask outright was one of only two things that clearly worked, so a take that adds a final “vote yes on 3” is the obvious test.

scripts.hook: 51% of Mass. races have been uncontested since 2014.
scripts.structure: Odds as a hook, the number said three ways, the consequence, who decided for you. No ask.
scripts.method: Stat-led and angry on purpose: a fact most viewers have not heard, anger at being chosen for, and the only script that never asks for the vote.

scripts.title: No Competition
scripts.framing: The calmest of the three, and the only one that names Question 3 directly.
scripts.source: Opening line from the Parallax library card; the rest drafted by PAX2 as a stand-in until the full script arrives
scripts.text:
More than half of Massachusetts races since 2014 have been completely uncontested. Think about that.
When there’s only one name on the ballot, there’s no debate, no comparison, and no reason for anyone to earn your vote.
Question 3 would put every candidate on one primary ballot, and the top finishers would move on to November. Every voter, in every party or none, gets a say.
That means real campaigns in the fall, with candidates who have to knock on doors, show up to debates, and explain where they stand.
It’s a simple change. More choices on the ballot, and representatives who have to answer to all of us.
Vote yes on Question 3.

why.note: Opens on the shared fact and tells the viewer to sit with it for a beat. The script explains before it argues — explaining facts held up in the tested ads; pure opinion didn't.

The mechanics in one sentence, which is where ballot measures live or die: on nine statewide votes, the simple versions passed (Washington 59.9%, California 53.7%) and the ones that took a paragraph to explain lost (Idaho 30.4%, South Dakota 34.4%).
What changes is told as things a viewer can picture — doors knocked, debates attended — not as process words.
The ask, plain and last: one of only two script features that clearly moved vote choice in the tests.

scripts.structure: The shared fact, why it matters, how Question 3 works in one line, what changes, the ask.
scripts.method: The plain explainer: facts explained, the mechanics in a sentence, pictures a viewer can see, and an explicit ask last.

scripts.title: No Need to Listen
scripts.framing: The accountability argument, with a plain-English analogy in the middle.
scripts.source: Opening line from the Parallax library card; the rest drafted by PAX2 as a stand-in until the full script arrives
scripts.text:
In most Massachusetts races, there’s no competition — one candidate, one party, no choice.
Why does that matter? Think about the only coffee shop in town. If nobody else can open across the street, prices go up and service goes down. Nobody has to try.
Politics works the same way. When politicians don’t have to compete, they don’t have to listen.
Since 2014, more than half of the races for the State House and Senate have had just one name on the ballot.
Question 3 changes the rules. Every candidate runs in one primary, and the top two finishers face off in November.
Two real choices in the fall means every vote has to be earned. That’s how you get representatives who actually listen.

why.note: The coffee-shop comparison does the arguing for the first half — an ordinary person talking the way people talk. Plain-folks delivery is the strongest vote-choice feature in the tested ads.
The thesis is a nine-word contrast: don't have to compete, don't have to listen. Contrast framing ran ahead on vote choice, short of proof.
One statistic in the whole script, held back until the comparison has made it make sense.
Ends one word short of “vote yes.” Whether saying it outright does better is exactly what the tests say to try.

scripts.hook: When politicians don't have to compete, they don't have to listen.
scripts.structure: The problem, a coffee-shop analogy, the thesis as a contrast, one statistic, the fix, the payoff.
scripts.method: Analogy and contrast in an ordinary voice; the single number held back until it makes sense; stops one word short of the ask.

scripts.title: Win a Majority
scripts.framing: The argument that polls best — for a viewer who wants to hear what voters actually support.
scripts.source: Written by PAX2 on the RealClear Opinion Research national poll (Jan 2026) and the uncontested-race returns
scripts.text:
Here’s a line from a national poll this January: open primaries would produce better candidates — candidates who appeal to a majority of voters, not just their base.
Seventy-three percent of voters agreed. Democrats, Republicans and independents — majorities of all three.
Now look at Massachusetts. In the last decade, nearly two-thirds of our state legislative races had exactly one name on the November ballot. Nobody had to appeal to a majority. Nobody had to appeal to anyone.
Question 3 is the fix: one primary, every candidate on it, every voter gets a ballot, and the top finishers go to November.
If you think candidates should have to win over a majority, this is how you make them.
Vote yes on Question 3.

why.note: Opens by reading the one argument for open primaries that has actually been message-tested, in the poll's own words — 73% of voters nationally agreed with it.
Names all three groups because the support really is cross-party — 79% of Democrats, 70% of independents, 65% of Republicans — so the claim is safe wherever the video lands.
Then the Massachusetts fact that makes the national argument local: 628 of the last 1,000 legislative races had one name on the ballot.
Mechanics in one sentence, like every script here — on statewide ballots the simple versions passed and the complicated ones lost.
The explicit ask — one of only two features that clearly moved vote choice in the tested ads.

scripts.hook: Candidates should have to win a majority.
scripts.structure: A poll result, who agreed, the local fact, the mechanics, the principle, the ask.
scripts.method: The polled argument: cross-party support first, a new local fact second, the explicit ask last.

scripts.title: Nobody's Party
scripts.framing: For the unenrolled viewer — two in three voters — who’s never felt a primary was theirs.
scripts.source: Written by PAX2 on the Aug 2026 enrollment figures and the uncontested-race returns
scripts.text:
Quick quiz. What’s the biggest political party in Massachusetts?
It’s not the Democrats — they’re twenty-four percent of registered voters. It’s not the Republicans — eight percent. It’s unenrolled: two out of every three of us belong to no party at all.
But primaries are still run party by party. You pick one ballot, you get a say in that one race — and by November, most races here have just one name left anyway.
Question 3 ends the sorting. One primary, every candidate on it, every voter gets the same ballot, and the top finishers move on.
Two-thirds of this state never joined a party. The election should work for them too.
Vote yes on 3.

why.note: A question the viewer will probably get wrong — the gap the next line fills. Curiosity openings won the randomized headline tests.
The registration facts, August 2026: 66.6% unenrolled, 24.5% Democrats, 8.0% Republicans. For most viewers this is news.

source.label: Secretary of the Commonwealth, via the Globe

why.note: Accurate on purpose: unenrolled voters can take a party ballot in Massachusetts, so the script claims only what's true — each voter gets a say in one party's race, while most Novembers end up with one name.
The explicit ask.

scripts.structure: A quiz, the surprising answer, the sorting problem, the fix, the principle, the ask.
scripts.method: A curiosity hook and a new fact aimed at the two in three voters who belong to no party; an explicit ask.

scripts.title: Your District
scripts.framing: Make it local: in 2022, 106 of the 160 House districts had one name on the ballot — check yours and say so.
scripts.source: Written by PAX2 on the 2022 Massachusetts House returns, district by district
scripts.text:
Quick question: who ran against your state rep in the last election?
If you can’t remember, here’s why. In 2022, one hundred six of the one hundred sixty Massachusetts House districts had exactly one name on the ballot. Two out of three.
Mine was one of them. No debate. No one knocking on my door. The election was over before it started.
Question 3 would change that: every candidate in one primary, every voter voting, and the top finishers facing off in November. Even a safe seat would have to be defended out loud.
Look up your district. If nobody ran against your rep either, now you know what to do about it.
Vote yes on Question 3.

why.note: Opens with a question most viewers can't answer about their own rep — and then answers it.
106 of 160, straight from the 2022 returns, said twice so it lands.

First person, as a neighbor — plain-folks delivery is the strongest vote-choice feature in the tested ads. Before recording, check the district list and make this line true for you; if your district had a race, cut it.
Hands the viewer something to do before the ask, then asks.

scripts.hook: Who ran against your rep? Probably nobody.
scripts.structure: A question about your own rep, the 106-of-160 fact, a first-person neighbor, the fix, something to do, the ask.
scripts.method: Local and first person, plain-folks delivery; a new fact said twice; an action before the ask.

scripts.title: Twenty Years
scripts.framing: For the skeptic who’s heard the case against: concede the strongest objection, then answer it.
scripts.source: Written by PAX2 on the statewide ballot history and the No side's own arguments
scripts.text:
The strongest argument against Question 3 is that it could put two candidates from the same party on the November ballot.
That’s true. It can.
Here’s what’s also true: in Massachusetts right now, nearly two-thirds of legislative races put ONE candidate on the November ballot. We skipped the two-of-the-same-party problem and went straight to none.
Washington has used a top-two primary since 2008, California since 2012. Hundreds of elections. It’s not an experiment anymore — it’s just how they vote.
And when two candidates from one party do face off, everyone else finally gets a say in which one wins.
Two names on every ballot, picked by everybody, beats one name picked for you.
Vote yes on Question 3.

why.note: Leads with the No side's best argument, stated fairly — the viewer who's already heard it knows this script isn't hiding from it.
The concession flips on a fact: today's system already produces one-name Novembers — 628 of the last 1,000 races. Built as a contrast, which ran ahead on vote choice.
The track record, from the ballot history: Washington passed it in 2004 with 59.9% and has voted that way since 2008; California passed it in 2010 with 53.7%.
The explicit ask.

scripts.hook: Washington has voted this way for nearly twenty years.
scripts.structure: The other side's best argument, the concession, the flip on a fact, the track record, the payoff, the ask.
scripts.method: Concede then answer, for the viewer who has heard the case against; contrast; the record in two states; an explicit ask.
